title.line2: Downtown Phoenix · ZIP 85004 · recorded live from the working product

end.line1: Real data. Real computation. Documented assumptions.

beats: Every downtown project raises two sets of questions.
The planning office asks whether it works for the streets and the neighbors.
Economic development asks what it does for jobs and the tax base.
Here's one proposal, answered for both.
This is ZIP code 85004, in downtown Phoenix, built from captured public data.
Census figures for the neighborhood sit right alongside it, with their margins of error.
Switch between 3D, plan, and satellite.
Click any building, and its sources are right there.
Now the proposal. Pick an apartment building, drop it on this open lot, and apply it.
Give this street a protected bike lane.
Every edit can be undone, and the before-and-after slider shows exactly what changed, on the same map.
The scorecard updates with every change.
This building adds forty-eight homes, and the trips they generate show up right away.
Click a number to see its formula, its inputs, and where they came from.
Starting values are labeled illustrative until your team replaces them with local figures.
For the planning office, attach FEMA's effective flood map, and every building is screened.
Here, no homes fall in FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area. That's a footprint screen, not a flood prediction.
Then housing. Search HUD's fiscal 2026 income limits for Phoenix.
These are the published limits by household size, so each group of homes can be followed through its full monthly cost.
For economic development: who can actually reach this site?
A real routing run measures the commute shed by car at fifteen, thirty, and forty-five minutes.
It reports Census education and occupation estimates for the people inside it, along with coverage and uncertainty.
A fiscal study starts from your jurisdiction's own levy and service costs, each one cited.
Retail gaps compare cited resident demand with local sales, one category at a time, and say so when a number is only an assumption.
Now the question everyone asks: traffic.
One click generates about two thousand synthetic car trips for the morning rush, and simulates them on the real street network.
It runs right here on this machine, and the result is saved to the scenario.
Synthetic rush-hour demand, real microscopic simulation.
These are the vehicles from that run, not an animation.
Zoom in, and you can follow individual cars along Central Avenue.
When it's time for the hearing, everything exports: Word, Excel, and GIS files.
The staff report has before-and-after maps, the scorecard, and the evidence.
One proposal, and one set of numbers both offices can work from.
